title: Runtime fragmentation healing and graceful OOM throttling
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Several customers across Hosted and Dedicated reported recurring GPU OOMs during long-running sessions and bursty multi-tenant workloads. Investigation shows a confluence of small KV handle leaks, uneven slab allocation, and allocator churn that together cause slow accumulation of unreachable allocations and fragmentation. This ticket tracks the engineering work to implement a two-pronged runtime change: (1) an opportunistic slab coalescer/compactor that runs during low-utilization windows to reduce fragmentation, and (2) a graceful OOM throttle and spill policy that prevents abrupt host-level OOMs by shedding low-priority sessions and checkpointing KV handles to spill storage when available.
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Start a mixed workload on a Hosted GPU pool with bursty chat sessions that keep KV cache warm for >6 hours
2) Toggle an aggresssive session retention policy with long prefix reuse (simulate conversational apps)
3) Observe increasing memory footprint over 12-36 hours with intermittent OOMs during short spikes
4) Run memory introspection (allocator slab histograms + KV handle counts) to see diverging slab occupancy and growing unreachable fragments
root_cause: No single catastrophic leak: small KV handle reference miscounts in the session reattach path combined with an allocator growth policy that allocates many small slabs for short-lived allocations. Over time these create fragmentation islands that the allocator cannot compact without global pauses. When burst traffic arrives, available contiguous GPU memory for large tensors is insufficient, causing OOMs. For some Private deployments, custom container cgroups magnify the effect by restricting transient reclaim windows.
mitigation_plan: Hotfix: introduce a soft-kill heuristic in the node agent to throttle new low-priority sessions when free contiguous GPU memory falls below threshold
Emergency operator playbook: evict stale sessions by LRU across tenant pools and restart affected runtime pods to reclaim top-level arena memory
Customer communication: notify impacted customers with suggested configuration (reduce session retention, increase eviction thresholds) while patch is rolled out
implementation_notes: Design a non-blocking slab coalescer that runs incrementally between request batches and limits per-epoch GPU kernel time to 2ms
Add KV handle weak-reference auditing in debug builds to identify miscount hotspots; do not enable by default in prod due to perf cost

Implement a pre-alloc snapshot-and-spill path: if allocator cannot satisfy large-contig request, attempt to spill least-recent KV entries to a per-tenant S3-backed cache (configurable and opt-in for Private)
rollout_plan: 1) Canary: Deploy coalescer + throttle to a single non-production Dedicated pool for 72h with increased observability
2) Gradual ramp: push to 10% of Hosted pools and a small set of Private customers who opt in; monitor OOM rate, tail latency, and KV eviction counts
3) Full rollout: after 7 days of stable canary metrics and sign-off from SRE, roll to all pools and include migration notes for on-prem operators
4) Emergency rollback path: disable --frag-coalesce-window-ms and revert oom-throttle to default behavior if P99 latency regresses >15%
qa_plan: Create a synthetic long-tail workload harness that reproduces slab islanding within 24h in CI Dedicated staging
Add unit tests for coalescer invariants (no memory corruption, bounded CPU/GPU time) and KV spill/reload correctness
Run end-to-end regression against the Hosted API compatibility suite to ensure no change in generation semantics
Performance test: compare per-token latency P50/P95/P99 and throughput before/after on target GPU types
